title: Isaiah 36:1–10
context: In Hezekiah’s fourteenth year (701 BC), Sennacherib has taken Judah’s fortified cities and sends his field commander, the Rabshakeh, to Jerusalem. Standing where Isaiah once met Ahaz, he mocks every source of Judah’s confidence: Egypt is a splintered reed, Hezekiah has offended the LORD by removing the high places, and the LORD himself has sent Assyria. Chapters 36–39 closely parallel 2 Kings 18–20.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Older voices from both traditions on Isaiah 36:1–10.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Sennacherib invades Judah. He sends Rabshakeh, who by his blasphemous persuasions tempts Hezekiah to despair, and the people to revolt. The history related here, and in the three following chapters, is, almost in the same words contained 2 Kings 18, 19, 20. It is inserted here, to explain and confirm some of the foregoing predictions. It may seem to have first been written by this prophet, and from him taken into the book of Kings, to compleat that history. Them—Many of them; universal particles being frequently so used both in scripture, and other authors; and this success God gave him; to lift him up to his own greater and more shameful destruction: to humble and chastise his own people for their manifold sins, and, to gain an eminent opportunity to advance his own honour by that miraculous deliverance which he designed for his people. Sent—Having received the money, upon which he agreed to depart from Hezekiah and his land, he breaks his faith with Hezekiah, thereby justifying his revolt, and preparing the way for his own destruction. Thus saith—But what are the greatest men when they come to compare with God, or when God comes to contend with them? This broken reed—Whoever trusts in man, leans on a broken reed: but God is the rock of ages. Is not—Thus boldly he speaks of the things which he understood not, judging of the great God, by their petty gods; and of God's worship by the vain fancies of the Heathens, who measured piety by the multitude of altars. Am I—He neither owned God's word, nor regarded his providence; but he forged this, to strike a terror into Hezekiah and the people.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Isa 36:1–10; 2 Kgs 18:13–25)

reformed.quote: It happened in the fourteenth year. In this and the following chapter the Prophet relates a remarkable history, which may be regarded as the seal of his doctrine, in which he predicted the calamities that would befall his nation, and at the same time promised that God would be merciful to them, and would drive back the Assyrians and defend Jerusalem and the Holy Land. Not without reason does he specify the time; for at that time Hezekiah had restored the worship of God throughout the whole of his dominions. While superstitions were removed and the Temple cleansed, Judea is invaded by the king of Assyria; Jerusalem alone is left, and in that city Hezekiah was shut up as in a prison. If we judge of this calamity according to the perception of the flesh, we shall think that God was unjust in permitting his servant to be reduced to such extremities; the Lord did not punish Hezekiah for carelessness, pleasures, or luxury, and much less for superstitions; God therefore intended to try his faith and patience. Yet the people were justly punished for their iniquities; although true religion flourished as to external worship, yet their life was not changed for the better. Then the king of Assyria sent Rabshakeh. Historical connection is frequently disturbed; the Scriptures frequently make use of a figure of speech in which a part is taken for the whole. Say now to Hezekiah: in order to terrify Hezekiah he calls the king of Assyria great; by these thunderbolts of words Hezekiah might have been overthrown. I have said (only a word of the lips): he ridicules Hezekiah, as if he fed the expectation of the people by empty boasting. Behold, thou hast trusted in that broken staff of reed: he slanderously and falsely accuses the pious king of this vain confidence; yet God justly rewarded a rebellious and disobedient people by allowing this filthy dog to reproach them with their wicked revolt. And if thou shalt say to me, We trust in Jehovah our God: this slander Satan attempted to wound the heart of the king; Hezekiah had taken away false gods and superstitious worship, which God abhors. Now come, give a hostage: this is ironical language. And how dost thou despise: Hezekiah ought not to be compared to the smallest of his captains. And now have I come up without Jehovah? He alleges that Hezekiah has not to contend with a mortal man, but with God himself. Satan assumes the character of God himself, and is transformed into an angel of light. We ought therefore to distinguish wisely when God speaks, and when, on the other hand, his name is falsely assumed by men. An upright conscience ought to be like a brazen wall to us, that, imitating the example of Hezekiah, we may stand unshaken against such accusations and slanders.

verses.text: Now in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria attacked all of the fortified cities of Judah and captured them.
verses.arminianNotes: Wesley: Sennacherib invades Judah. The history related here is, almost in the same words contained 2 Kings 18, 19, 20. It is inserted here, to explain and confirm some of the foregoing predictions. Them—many of them; universal particles being frequently so used both in scripture, and other authors; and this success God gave him; to lift him up to his own greater and more shameful destruction: to humble and chastise his own people for their manifold sins, and, to gain an eminent opportunity to advance his own honour by that miraculous deliverance which he designed for his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: in this and the following chapter the Prophet relates a remarkable history, which may be regarded as the seal of his doctrine. Not without reason does he specify the time; for at that time Hezekiah had restored the worship of God. If we judge of this calamity according to the perception of the flesh, we shall think that God was unjust in permitting his servant to be reduced to such extremities; the Lord did not punish Hezekiah for carelessness, pleasures, or luxury; God therefore intended to try his faith and patience. Yet the people were justly punished for their iniquities; although true religion flourished as to external worship, yet their life was not changed for the better.
verses.keyContrast: Both keep Sennacherib’s coming as in Hezekiah’s fourteenth year. Wesley reads “all” as many of them, universal particles so used; God gave the success to lift Assyria toward a more shameful destruction, to humble and chastise his own people for their manifold sins, and to gain an eminent opportunity to advance his own honour by the miraculous deliverance he designed. Calvin reads the narrative as the seal of Isaiah’s doctrine; Hezekiah’s piety is tried, not punished for superstition; the people, not the reforming king, are chastised for unchanged lives.

verses.text: The king of Assyria sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem to King Hezekiah with a large army. He stood by the aqueduct from the upper pool in the fuller’s field highway.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: sent—having received the money, upon which he agreed to depart from Hezekiah and his land, he breaks his faith with Hezekiah, thereby justifying his revolt, and preparing the way for his own destruction.

Rabshakeh stands at the very spot where Isaiah had met Ahaz (7:3). Wesley notes that Sennacherib took Hezekiah’s money and marched anyway, breaking faith and preparing his own downfall.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: then the king of Assyria sent Rabshakeh. The order of the narrative may here have been altered; historical connection is frequently disturbed; the Scriptures frequently make use of a figure of speech in which a part is taken for the whole. It appeared that the king of Assyria had brought the whole of Judea under his dominion, because nearly all that remained was Jerusalem alone, in which Hezekiah was shut up.

The great army stays with Lachish’s siege.”

verses.text: Then Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah, the son of Asaph the recorder came out to him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley (on v. 2): he sends Rabshakeh, who by his blasphemous persuasions tempts Hezekiah to despair, and the people to revolt. Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah come out; the history is inserted here to explain and confirm some of the foregoing predictions.

Hezekiah sends his three senior officials to meet Rabshakeh, the same men who will bring the report back in torn clothes (v. 22).
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: Eliakim was formerly mentioned. It was he to whom the Lord promised that he would give him the chief power in the kingdom after the banishment of Shebna. It now appears as if that promise had failed, when he is sent to an enemy as a suppliant. Besides, the godly king had such a scarcity of good men, that, along with Eliakim, he was compelled to send Shebna, whom he knew well to be deceitful and treacherous.

Calvin will not let Isa 22’s promise look failed because Eliakim walks out as a suppliant.

verses.text: Rabshakeh said to them, “Now tell Hezekiah, ‘The great king, the king of Assyria, says, “What confidence is this in which you trust?
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: thus saith—but what are the greatest men when they come to compare with God, or when God comes to contend with them?

“What confidence is this?” The whole speech turns on trust. Wesley answers that even the “great king” is small beside God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: say now to Hezekiah. The three ambassadors were not only repulsed, but disdainfully treated by the tyrant’s delegate. Thus saith the great king: he calls the king of Assyria great, because by his power he eclipsed all others, so that he stood alone in his lofty rank. By these thunderbolts of words Hezekiah might have been overthrown and subdued.

The “great king” stays a taunt.

verses.text: I say that your counsel and strength for the war are only vain words. Now in whom do you trust, that you have rebelled against me?
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: what are the greatest men when they come to compare with God, or when God comes to contend with them?

Rabshakeh’s question—“In whom do you trust?”—is the right question asked with the wrong intent. Arminian readers note that the taunt forces Judah to name its confidence.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: I have said (only a word of the lips). He ridicules Hezekiah, as if he fed the expectation of the people by empty boasting, while he was not provided with military preparations. He perfectly understands, he claims, what it is on which Hezekiah places his chief reliance, namely, on words and eloquence; but it is not by these that war can be begun or carried on.

verses.text: Behold, you trust in the staff of this bruised reed, even in Egypt, which if a man leans on it, it will go into his hand and pierce it. So is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: this broken reed—whoever trusts in man, leans on a broken reed: but God is the rock of ages.

Egypt is a splintered reed that pierces the hand of anyone who leans on it. Rabshakeh is right about Egypt; he is wrong in thinking Judah has nothing else to lean on.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: behold, thou hast trusted in that broken staff of reed. He slanderously and falsely accuses the pious king of this vain confidence. Yet God justly rewarded a rebellious and disobedient people by allowing this filthy dog to reproach them with their wicked revolt. The hope of receiving aid from the Egyptians is not only false and unfounded, but pernicious.

Calvin does not let the slander stand as if the pious king had leaned on Egypt; the reed is Rabshakeh’s taunt, not Hezekiah’s policy.
verses.keyContrast: Both keep Egypt as that broken reed at the wall. Wesley reads a pastoral rule: whoever trusts in man leans on a broken reed; but God is the rock of ages. Calvin reads the same reed as a slander of Hezekiah: the pious king did not rest on Egypt; Rabshakeh falsely accuses him, though the people deserved the taunt for their revolt.

verses.text: But if you tell me, ‘We trust in the LORD our God,’ isn’t that he whose high places and whose altars Hezekiah has taken away, and has said to Judah and to Jerusalem, ‘You shall worship before this altar’?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: is not—thus boldly he speaks of the things which he understood not, judging of the great God, by their petty gods; and of God's worship by the vain fancies of the Heathens, who measured piety by the multitude of altars.

Rabshakeh mistakes Hezekiah’s reform for sacrilege: removing the high places, he thinks, must have offended Israel’s God. Wesley calls it judging the great God by petty gods.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: this slander Satan attempted not only to wound the heart of the king. Every person must plainly see how slanderous is that charge; for Hezekiah had taken away false gods and superstitious worship, which God abhors. We must stand out with unshaken faith against such ungodly speeches, by shewing that what they call the worship of God is not his worship.

Calvin and Wesley both keep Rabshakeh ignorant of the LORD’s worship.

verses.text: Now therefore, please make a pledge to my master the king of Assyria, and I will give you two thousand horses, if you are able on your part to set riders on them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley (on v. 6): whoever trusts in man, leans on a broken reed: but God is the rock of ages.

The wager mocks Judah’s weakness: they could not even find riders for two thousand horses. The insult is meant to make trust in God look absurd.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: now come, give a hostage. He concludes that there will be nothing better for Hezekiah than to lay aside the intention of carrying on war and to surrender. This is ironical language. If I shall give thee two thousand horses, thou wilt not find among all thy people men to ride on them.

The wager stays a taunt.”

verses.text: How then can you turn away the face of one captain of the least of my master’s servants, and put your trust in Egypt for chariots and for horsemen?
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley (on the reed of v. 6): whoever trusts in man, leans on a broken reed: but God is the rock of ages.

The taunt measures Judah’s weakness against one minor captain. Wesley answers that whoever trusts in man leans on a broken reed, while God is the rock of ages.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: and how dost thou despise? Hezekiah is so far from being able to endure the presence of his king, that he ought not to be compared to the very smallest of his captains. Although Sennacherib does not yet appear before them with his whole army, Rabshakeh boasts that his lieutenants are sufficiently powerful, so that Hezekiah ought not to hesitate to make submission.

verses.text: Have I come up now without the LORD against this land to destroy it? The LORD said to me, “Go up against this land, and destroy it.”’”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: am I—he neither owned God's word, nor regarded his providence; but he forged this, to strike a terror into Hezekiah and the people.

Rabshakeh claims the LORD sent him. Wesley calls it a forgery meant to terrify—though Isaiah had indeed called Assyria the rod of God’s anger (10:5), Assyria never knew it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: and now have I come up without Jehovah? He alleges that Hezekiah has not to contend with a mortal man, but with God himself. Satan assumes the character of God himself, and is transformed into an angel of light. We ought therefore to distinguish wisely when God speaks, and when, on the other hand, his name is falsely assumed by men. An upright conscience ought to be like a brazen wall, that, imitating Hezekiah, we may stand unshaken.

Calvin does not let “the LORD said” pass as God’s mouth.
verses.keyContrast: Both keep “the LORD said, Go up against this land” as Rabshakeh’s word at that wall. Wesley reads a forgery: he neither owned God's word, nor regarded his providence; he forged this to strike a terror into Hezekiah and the people. Calvin reads a subtler theft of the Name: Satan assumes the character of God and is transformed into an angel of light; we must distinguish when God speaks from when men falsely assume his name.
